items.title: Zelenskiy criticizes Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ’wrong’

events.article_text:
India is the largest importer of Russian seaborne crude, averaging 1.8 million barrels per day this year, ahead of China at 1.2 million, ship tracking data showed

India is expected to keep importing Russian crude at close to current levels after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs mandated by a new law on major buyers of Russian oil, analysts said.

Trump issued an executive order late on Friday waiving the "sanctions, restrictions, and duties" under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a day before a 30-day deadline for enforcement expired. He signed the law on September 18.

The law authorised tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude and gas, and sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet of tankers. The waiver is not specific to India and could also benefit China. The order lets the administration reconsider it later.

India took about 1.82 million bpd of Russian crude in September against about 1.49 million for China. Kpler expects October imports to hold at around 1.8-1.9 million bpd. Volumes are well below mid-year highs. Indian imports peaked at 2.6 million bpd in June and 2.57 million bpd in July.

With the waiver, refiners are likely to continue buying Russian crude, analysts said.

Russian crude emerged as a bargain for Indian refiners after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered Western sanctions and prompted many buyers to shun its oil. The European Union banned seaborne imports of Russian crude, while the G7 imposed a price cap aimed at curbing Moscow's oil revenues without disrupting global supplies.

With traditional buyers retreating, Russia redirected cargoes to Asia at steep discounts to benchmark Brent crude, at times approaching USD 40 a barrel for its Urals grade in early 2023.

India seized the opportunity, transforming its crude sourcing in a matter of months. Russian oil accounted for around 2 per cent or less of India's imports before the war, but refiners rapidly increased purchases as discounted cargoes improved processing economics and helped contain the cost of imported energy.

Russia went on to become India's largest crude supplier, at times accounting for around 40-50 per cent of the country's total imports.

The shift also created a lucrative export stream for Indian refiners, which processed Russian crude into fuels such as diesel for domestic consumption and overseas markets. Although purchases have fluctuated with prices, supply availability and geopolitical pressures, the rapid rise of Russian oil has fundamentally reshaped India's crude import mix, analysts said.

The discounts made Russian oil an attractive alternative to supplies from West Asia and other producers, they said, adding that Russia made up for volumes that were lost due to the Iran war disrupting supplies earlier this year.

In September 2026, the price discount on Urals-grade crude oil relative to the global benchmark Brent averaged USD 23 per barrel, analysts said.

The latest sanctions waiver follows a Treasury decision on October 9 to allow the sale and import of Russian diesel into the global market, including the US, until April 7, 2027. The diesel waiver made enforcement of the new law unlikely, analysts said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

analysis.tldr: US President Donald Trump has waived potential penalties on buyers of Russian oil, meaning Indian refiners can keep importing discounted Russian crude without fear of American tariffs.
the_story: US President Donald Trump issued an executive order on Friday waiving sanctions, restrictions, and duties under a new law targeting major buyers of Russian oil, avoiding a 30-day enforcement deadline.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act had authorized tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the top five importers of Russian crude and gas, and sanctions on Russia's shadow tanker fleet.
India is currently the largest importer of Russian seaborne crude, averaging 1.8 million barrels per day this year, ahead of China at 1.2 million, according to ship tracking data from Kpler.
Russian oil became a bargain for Indian refiners after Western sanctions following the Ukraine invasion in February 2022, saving import costs and helping make Russia India's largest crude supplier.
In September 2026, the price discount on Russia's Urals-grade crude relative to the global benchmark Brent averaged USD 23 per barrel.
analysis.what_happened: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving harsh tariffs and penalties that were threatened against major buyers of Russian oil. This happened just before a 30-day enforcement window closed, preventing sudden trade restrictions on countries like India that buy large amounts of Russian crude.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop getting official permission to keep buying discounted vegetables from a controversial wholesaler, meaning they can continue selling cheaper food to their customers without the local authorities fining them.
why_it_matters_india: US President Donald Trump waives sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, removing the threat of up to 100% tariffs on Indian imports.

Indian refiners can safely continue purchasing discounted Russian crude (which averaged a USD 23 per barrel discount to Brent in September 2026) at current levels of around 1.8 million barrels per day.
Lower raw material costs for oil refiners keep processing economics favorable and help contain the cost of imported energy for the country.
Stabilized energy import costs reduce pressure on domestic fuel prices and help cushion the Indian rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) from sudden imported inflation shocks.

impacts.rationale: Continued access to heavily discounted Russian oil (USD 23 per barrel discount in September) keeps refining costs lower, which is good for everyday consumers at the pump.
Avoiding severe US tariff penalties and maintaining steady energy import costs prevents sudden drains on India's foreign exchange reserves, which supports a stronger rupee — good for cheaper imports.
Stable and cheaper energy imports prevent broader price hikes across goods and services, which is good for household budgets.

watch_next: Whether the US administration decides to reconsider or lift the sanctions waiver later on
Monthly ship tracking data on whether Indian imports of Russian crude stay between 1.8 and 1.9 million barrels per day
analysis.caveats: The executive order explicitly notes that the administration can reconsider the waiver later, meaning policy could shift if geopolitical pressures change.

events.article_text:
U.S. Offers Another 17 Million SPR Barrels as Fuel Crisis Deepens

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

During the first three months or so of the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, the dominant mood on oil markets was that the conflict would end any day now. The brief June ceasefire reinforced that optimism, so it took a while longer for facts to be faced: the war would not end any day now. It might even extend into next year—and this means higher prices for a longer time.

The ICE Brent crude futures contract for January 2027 is trading at $102.59 per barrel. The June 2027 contract is only slightly lower, at $92.71 per barrel, and the December 2027 contract is trading at $84.75 per barrel. For context, in December 2025, Brent crude was trading at less than $70 per barrel. Back in March, most oil market observers and players seemed to expect prices to retreat from their war-fueled highs fast. Now, those who use oil seem to expect supply to remain tight, and they are hedging their future consumption at higher prices.

Even the multiple reports of oil flows out of the Persian Gulf recovering to pre-war levels—and even topping pre-war levels—did not help bring prices down for very long. That is, first, because there is a crisis of trust in the official figures reported, and second, because the recovery in flows, such as it is, depends on costly maneuvers such as ship-to-ship transfers that have tightened the tanker market, led to surging freight costs, and forced Gulf producers to discount their crude to keep demand steady. Meanwhile, Iran is striking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on an almost daily basis. The war premium on oil remains very much in place. Related: Global Gas Crunch Makes Europe’s Remaining Coal Plants Profitable

In refined fuels, the situation is even more challenging, especially in diesel. Those outlets that reported the almost total recovery in oil flows out of Hormuz did not have the same news about fuel flows, because so many refineries in the Middle East became targets in Iran’s retaliatory strikes. The world’s fuel supply is tight and getting tighter by the day.

The International Energy Agency said this week it will begin releasing more than 20 million barrels of diesel from collective inventory to help fill the supply gap that has pushed prices to all-time highs. The total diesel release could reach 50 million barrels, or half of the total inventory release IEA members agreed earlier this month under tariff pressure from President Trump. The problem with inventory releases is that sooner or later they will run out—and replenishment will be difficult because the world is, quite plainly, short on refining capacity.

Despite these developments, the IEA appears to still believe peace between the United States, Israel, and Iran, is only a matter of time. Indeed, the agency said in its latest monthly oil report it expected global oil supply to rebound to 108.3 million barrels daily, from less than 101 million barrels daily this year. This would mean an increase of over 7 million barrels daily—and this would mean that oil flows out of the Middle East have not, in fact, recovered to pre-war levels, not to mention LNG flows.

All this means that inflationary pressures driven by the high cost of energy commodities would continue to weigh on the global economy for a longer period than initially hoped. Central bankers are already getting nervous, and so are governments. There is only a limited number of options of how to handle such a situation, and most of them involve spending tax money on temporary relief at the pump. That, however, cannot continue forever, and it especially cannot continue for very long in a state of economic stagnation or even recession.

For now, official global economic growth forecasts appear upbeat. The International Monetary Fund earlier this week said the global economy could expand by a pretty decent 3.4% next year thanks to its resilience. However, the lender’s chief economist warned that “The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding. We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience,” Silvana Tenreyro said.

However, rebuilding normally begins once the hostilities are over, and the hostilities in the Middle East—and Russia and Ukraine, for that matter—are very much ongoing, and the outlook is uncertain for both. It seems that for now, the world will need to continue coping rather than rebuilding, and get used to costlier energy across the board for the observable future—much costlier. The ICE low-sulfur gasoil futures contract for November is trading at over $1,404 per ton. The contract for December 2027 is trading at $1,001 per ton. Things in oil and gas are not coming back to normal in a few days, not even in a few weeks.

analysis.tldr: Prolonged war in the Middle East means expensive crude oil and diesel will stay for a long time, making everyday goods and transport costlier for Indians.
the_story: The ongoing war involving the US, Israel, and Iran is extending into next year, keeping oil supply tight and prices high.
Brent crude futures for January 2027 are trading at $102.59 per barrel, up significantly from under $70 in December 2025.
Iran is striking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz almost daily and targeting Middle Eastern refineries, leading to soaring freight costs and a severe diesel shortage.

The International Energy Agency (the IEA, a group of countries that works to ensure reliable energy) is releasing emergency diesel inventories, but warned that supplies will eventually run out due to a lack of global refining capacity.
analysis.what_happened: Ongoing conflicts in the Middle East have disrupted oil and fuel supply chains longer than expected, causing markets to accept that high prices are here to stay. Because oil tankers face attacks and regional refineries are damaged, getting fuel to the rest of the world has become difficult and expensive.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop running short on flour because the delivery trucks keep getting blocked—the store has to charge much higher prices for whatever stock is left, and customers have no choice but to pay up.
why_it_matters_india: Conflict risk rises in the Middle East -> Oil supply remains tight and expensive globally.
India imports the vast majority of its crude oil -> Costlier imports drain foreign currency reserves.
More dollars leave India to pay for expensive oil -> The rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Costlier fuel raises transportation and manufacturing costs -> Domestic inflation (rising prices of everyday goods) increases for common people.

impacts.rationale: Persistent war and damaged Middle East refineries keep supply constrained, which is bad for consumers as it keeps energy costs high.
India has to spend more dollars to buy expensive oil, weakening the rupee, which makes all imported goods costlier for regular people.
Higher fuel prices push up transport and production costs across the board, leading to more expensive goods and services—bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Updates on security conditions and oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz
Decisions by international agencies regarding further emergency oil and diesel inventory releases
analysis.caveats: If a lasting ceasefire is unexpectedly reached in the Middle East, oil prices could drop much faster than current futures contracts suggest.

These measures include tightening foreign exchange derivative norms and creating a special window for oil marketing companies. The impact of these interventions is expected to affect the rupee's value and forward premiums.

analysis.tldr: When the Reserve Bank of India steps in to defend the rupee, it helps stop the local currency from dropping further, which keeps imported items like crude oil from suddenly getting much costlier for everyday consumers.
the_story: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) [India's central banking institution] announced new steps to stabilize the rupee's value in foreign exchange markets.

The central bank is tightening foreign exchange derivative norms [rules for financial contracts whose value depends on currency prices] by implementing a cash reserve requirement for large forex derivatives.
The RBI is creating a special window for oil marketing companies to help manage their dollar needs.
These interventions are designed to curb speculative dollar demand and will affect the rupee's value and forward premiums [the extra cost to buy a currency for future delivery].
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India stepped into the market because the rupee was getting very close to hitting a record low. To stop this slide, the central bank tightened rules on financial contracts tied to foreign currencies and made it harder for people to make risky bets against the rupee.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper stepping in to stop customers from hoarding milk during a shortage, making sure there is enough to go around without the price spiking wildly.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI tightens rules and creates a special window for oil companies to buy dollars -> Speculative betting against the local currency drops -> The downward pressure on the rupee eases -> Imported goods like crude oil avoid extreme price surges, which helps control local inflation.

The central bank restricts certain foreign exchange derivative contracts -> The demand for buying US dollars speculatively falls -> The rupee receives artificial support against further steep declines.

impacts.rationale: Direct RBI intervention and stricter rules slow down the currency's fall, which is generally good because it prevents imported goods from becoming suddenly expensive.
A steadier rupee makes buying essential imports like crude oil slightly more predictable, helping keep everyday price rises in check — good for household budgets.
By helping oil companies manage their dollar needs smoothly, extreme currency shocks that push up fuel prices are avoided, which benefits ordinary drivers.

watch_next: Whether the rupee holds its ground or continues sliding toward historic lows
Further actions or statements from the Reserve Bank of India on foreign exchange rules
analysis.caveats: If global demand for the US dollar remains extremely high, even aggressive central bank rules might only slow down the rupee's decline rather than completely reverse it.

events.headline: Analysis: Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Hormuz crisis

items.title: Analysis: Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Hormuz crisis
items.summary: The UK has avoided the need for gas imports worth £5.9bn since the start of the Hormuz crisis as a… The post Analysis: Wind and solar save UK from gas imports worth £5.9bn during Hormuz crisis appeared first on Carbon Brief .

events.article_text:
The UK has avoided the need for gas imports worth £5.9bn since the start of the Hormuz crisis as a result of record generation from wind and solar, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

While gas prices are surging to levels not seen since the 2022 energy crisis, the UK has been generating record amounts of power from wind and solar, up 14% year-on-year.

This unprecedented clean-power generation is directly cutting the need for gas-fired electricity, which is down by nearly 10% year-on-year in 2026 to date.

In total, wind and solar have generated a record 41% share of the UK’s electricity needs in 2026 to date, compared with 25% from gas, according to Carbon Brief’s analysis.

The figure below shows that wind and solar has avoided the need for UK gas imports worth £5.9bn, since the outbreak of war between the US and Iran in February 2026.

These avoided gas imports would have required the UK to secure the equivalent of more than 100 additional tanker deliveries of liquefied natural gas (LNG).

The £1.3bn import saving in September 2026 to date is the result of record wind and solar output, at nearly 10 terawatt hours (TWh), combined with surging gas prices.

The latest analysis updates figures published by Carbon Brief in April and May.

Wholesale gas prices in the UK have remained elevated ever since Russia cut off supplies to Europe in the wake of its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Gas averaged 90p per therm from 2023 until the start of this year, roughly three times above 2019 prices, before the Covid and Ukraine crises.

Since the outbreak of war in the Middle East in March, gas prices have climbed higher still, averaging 134p per therm or nearly four times the level seen in 2019.

In September 2026 to date, gas prices have averaged 189p per therm, reaching their highest level since the global energy crisis in 2022, as shown in the figure below.

UK gas prices are spiking again because winter is approaching – meaning higher demand for heating – and there is no end in sight for the Hormuz crisis.

At the same time, European gas stocks are low. This means Europe will have to compete with Asia to secure the cargoes of LNG needed to keep warm.

In the UK, high wholesale gas prices are hitting household gas bills under the price cap set by energy regulator Ofgem, whereas electricity bills have barely increased.

From this Thursday, 1 October, typical household gas bills will be 33% higher than they were in April, some £200 per year, according to thinktank Nesta.

In contrast, household electricity bills will only have risen 4%, according to Nesta’s analysis, as a result of growing generation from clean-energy sources.

Andrew Sissons, director for sustainable future at Nesta, explained in a social media post that “the link between electricity and gas prices has already begun to break”.

The UK and other fossil-fuel importing nations are being hit not only by high gas prices, but also by high prices for oil, diesel and other refined fuels.

The EU has reportedly had to pay an extra €100bn for fossil-fuel imports since the start of the crisis. Higher import bills have fallen particularly hard on low and middle-income countries, according to separate analysis.

In the UK, diesel prices have hit record levels of around £2 per litre. In contrast, recent Carbon Brief analysis shows that electric cars are up to nine times cheaper to drive.

In her speech to the Labour party conference, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said that energy bills were high because the UK is “exposed to global fossil-fuel markets”.

In his own conference speech, prime minister Andy Burnham said the expansion of clean energy was easing the impact of high gas prices on electricity bills. He said:

“We are already taking more control of our electricity prices with a massive expansion of home-grown renewables and nuclear. I have asked Miatta to speed up the breaking of the link between what we pay for power at home and the international gas market, to get bills down.”

analysis.tldr: When global gas and oil prices spike due to conflicts abroad, India faces costlier imported fuel and higher domestic inflation.
the_story: The UK avoided £5.9bn in gas imports during the Hormuz crisis because wind and solar generated a record 41% of its electricity in 2026.
UK gas prices hit their highest level since the 2022 energy crisis, averaging 189p per therm in September 2026, driven by the Middle East war, winter demand, and low European gas stocks.
UK household gas bills are jumping 33% (£200 per year) under the Ofgem [energy regulator] price cap, while electricity bills rose only 4% thanks to renewable energy.
Fossil-fuel importing nations face high prices for oil and diesel, with UK diesel hitting record levels of around £2 per litre.
analysis.what_happened: A war in the Middle East near the Strait of Hormuz has pushed global natural gas and oil prices to surge. However, the UK softened this blow by generating record amounts of electricity from wind and solar, cutting its need for expensive gas imports.
analysis.analogy: It is like having solar panels on your roof that keep your electricity bill low, even when the price of coal or gas used by the main power grid shoots through the roof.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East conflicts and supply disruptions drive up global crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices.
Because India imports a vast majority of its oil and gas, higher global prices increase the import bill for the country.
Costlier imported energy feeds into higher domestic fuel and transport costs, raising overall inflation (the rate at which prices rise).
A wider trade deficit (when imports cost more than exports) can put downward pressure on the Indian rupee.

impacts.rationale: higher global energy and gas prices make transport and goods more expensive, which is bad for household budgets
costlier imported fuel means India needs more dollars to buy energy, weakening the local currency, which makes all imports pricier
global refined fuel and oil price surges usually translate to higher pump prices in importing nations like India, hurting everyday commuters

watch_next: Developments in the Middle East and the Strait of Hormuz shipping route
Global spot prices for liquefied natural gas (LNG) and crude oil
India's monthly trade deficit and oil import bill reports
analysis.caveats: Global energy prices can swing rapidly depending on unexpected diplomatic resolutions or further escalations in the Middle East.

analysis.analogy: It is like three local businesses finally passing all health and safety checks so they can open their doors and invite the neighborhood to become part-owners by buying a slice of the shop.
why_it_matters_india: Sebi approves IPOs for Cult.fit, Eswari Global Metal, and Sohan Lal Commodity ->
These companies prepare to invite public subscriptions [people applying to buy shares] ->
Retail investors (ordinary people investing small sums) and FIIs (big foreign institutional investors) evaluate these new shares ->
Money flows from investors into these newly listed companies, changing market activity.

impacts.rationale: More public listings bring excitement and fresh money into the broader stock market, which can be generally good for market sentiment.

The price band [the set price range at which shares are offered] fixed by each company

events.headline: WTO and multilateral partners review progress on supply chain finance initiative

items.title: WTO and multilateral partners review progress on supply chain finance initiative
items.summary: Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala joined leaders of multilateral development banks and other international organizations at a high-level roundtable held on the sidelines of the 2026 World Bank – International Monetary Fund (IMF) Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on 16 October to review progress in expanding supply chain finance in developing economies and to discuss priorities for the next phase of cooperation.

events.article_text:
The discussion, organized jointly by the WTO and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), built on commitments made in the 2024 joint statement on Boosting Supply Chain Trade in Emerging Markets. Participants assessed developments since the launch of the initiative and examined how the current global trade and economic environment is affecting access to supply chain finance, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in low-income and vulnerable economies.

Opening the meeting, DG Okonjo-Iweala highlighted the importance of supply chain finance in helping firms participate in international trade and integrate into regional and global value chains.

She said: "Expanding access to supply chain finance is essential to ensuring that smaller businesses can seize trade opportunities and contribute to economic growth. By working together, multilateral institutions can help address persistent financing gaps and support more inclusive participation in global trade."

IFC's Managing Director and Executive Vice President, Makhtar Diop, who co-chaired the event, said: "Supply chain finance can have a transformative impact on trade flows and emerging market economies when the right elements come together: capital, legal infrastructure, digital platforms, and the market capacity to put it to work. Together, multilateral development banks (MDBs) are uniquely positioned to strengthen regulatory and market conditions and leverage our own capital to mobilize private investment at scale, channeling it to smaller businesses and markets where access to finance remains out of reach."

Participants reviewed work undertaken since 2024 to help SMEs overcome the barriers they face in obtaining trade-related financing. This work has included expanding supply chain finance programmes, strengthening legal and regulatory frameworks, promoting market infrastructure, building institutional capacity and broadening the range of financing products available to businesses.

Supply chain finance helps support SMEs' participation in trade by providing affordable financing that improves firms' cash flow. Direct financing provided by multilateral development banks has grown from about USD 35 billion annually before the COVID-19 to about USD 65 billion in 2026, benefiting both low and middle-income countries. Of this, USD 10 billion corresponds to supply chain finance in developing economies, which represents a two-to-threefold increase from 2024.

The roundtable also explored ways to mobilize greater private-sector participation and investment in supply chain finance markets. Participants also discussed practical measures for broadening access to underserved markets and improving SMEs' resilience in supply chains. This includes local currency financing for product innovation, partnerships, capacity-building and financial product awareness.

Participants reaffirmed their commitment to enhancing cooperation through the existing Supply Chain Finance Task Force under the WTO's Multilateral Development Banks Working Group. The Task Force coordinates action across multilateral development banks, namely the International Finance Corporation (World Bank Group), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank, the Afreximbank, the Inter-American Development Bank and the Islamic Trade Finance Corporation (Islamic Development Bank Group). Multilateral development banks coordinate with the WTO Secretariat and with private sector institutions, such as the International Chamber of Commerce and FCI, the global representative body for the factoring and receivables finance industry.

The Working Group agreed at the roundtable to continue coordinating efforts aimed at expanding financing opportunities in developing economies.

The roundtable brought together senior representatives from multilateral development banks and international organizations participating in the supply chain finance initiative.

analysis.tldr: Global organizations are scaling up affordable short-term loans for small businesses trading internationally, which could indirectly ease export credit access for Indian small and medium businesses.
the_story: The World Trade Organization (WTO) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) jointly organized a discussion to review progress on their supply chain finance initiative launched in 2024.

Direct financing by multilateral development banks (MDBs) has grown from about USD 35 billion annually before COVID-19 to about USD 65 billion in 2026, with USD 10 billion dedicated to supply chain finance in developing economies.

Participants included major global financial institutions like the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank, and the Islamic Trade Finance Corporation, coordinating through the WTO's Multilateral Development Banks Working Group.
analysis.what_happened: Major international organizations met to review how well they are helping small businesses in developing economies get short-term loans to buy and sell goods globally. They reported that overall funding from international development banks has nearly doubled compared to pre-pandemic levels, driven by a push to fix financing gaps for smaller companies.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of wealthy uncles pooling their money to help local shopkeepers get small loans to buy inventory, making it easier for them to stock their shelves and run their businesses.
why_it_matters_india: International development banks expand supply chain funding pools -> More credit flows to emerging market trade networks
Indian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs [smaller businesses]) engaged in exports gain better access to affordable working capital loans
Easier cash flow management helps Indian smaller exporters participate more deeply in global supply chains
Broader global trade liquidity supports overall export volumes from developing countries including India

impacts.rationale: Smoother global supply chains can marginally reduce import and production bottlenecks, which is generally good for keeping everyday consumer prices stable.
Better financing for smaller exporting companies can support overall manufacturing and export growth, mildly benefiting broader market sentiment.

watch_next: Specific funding announcements and credit lines from institutions like the Asian Development Bank targeting Indian exporters
Changes in credit availability for small and medium-sized manufacturing firms in India
analysis.caveats: This is a broad policy and financing coordination meeting, so direct impacts on individual Indian businesses will depend heavily on how fast local partner banks distribute these funds.

events.headline: Exercise Tarang Shakti: A Mirror to India’s Multipronged Engagements

items.title: Exercise Tarang Shakti: A Mirror to India’s Multipronged Engagements
items.summary: The exercise reflects two trends: the Indian military’s deepening interoperability with key partner nations, and India’s multi-vector foreign policy.

events.article_text:
“The defense relationships of the future will be about technology and trust, not just about platforms,” India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said at an event and demonstration in Jodhpur on October 10 as the multilateral Exercise Tarang Shakti neared its end. A fly-past after that featured an arrow-shaped formation that included the Indian Air Force Su-30MKI (Russian origin) at the center, flanked on one side by a U.S. F-35 and an Indian Light Combat Aircraft (LCA), and on the other side by a French Rafale and an F-16 of the United Arab Emirates Air Force. This was an impressive formation; the technology and firepower they represented cannot be easily beaten.

An American fifth-generation fighter flying alongside a Russian-origin jet bears testimony to India’s multi-pronged foreign policy and military engagements.

Beyond Tarang Shakti, some bilateral exercises have culminated while others are lined up, showcasing the busy calendar of India’s military diplomacy and military-to-military engagements. For instance, at Vladivostok in Russia, the Indian and Russian Navies are holding their annual Indra exercise from October 13 to 18.

Together, these reflect two trends: one is the Indian military’s deepening interoperability across land, sea and air with key partner nations and like-minded countries, and the other is India’s multi-vectored foreign policy in line with its much-espoused strategic autonomy.

A biennial exercise, Tarang Shakti is now in its second edition. It was themed “Power in Partnership” and was held at Jodhpur near India’s western borders. It commenced on September 26 and ended on October 12. It brought together the Indian Air Force (IAF) and seven other countries – Australia, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, the UAE, and the U.S. – who deployed their aerial assets. Thirty-two other nations participated as observers.

The real metric of an exercise’s utility is not what the host nation deploys but what partner nations bring in, reflective of the value they see from it. The U.S. fifth-generation F-35 jets exercised over Indian skies for the first time, operating alongside the entire gamut of IAF fighters – the LCA, Rafale, SU-30MKI, Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars, French Rafales and the UAE’s F-16s. These were completed by A-400M and C-130/ C-130J transport aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, G-6000 and other support platforms. An IAF official, citing a post-exercise data brief, told The Diplomat that Tarang Shakti saw more than 800 sorties and 600 hours flown.

The U.S. Pacific Air Forces deployed six F-35A Lightning IIs and one KC-135R Stratotanker along with over 200 personnel. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, U.S. Ambassador in India Sergio Gor remarked that their F-35s do not go all over the world and termed their presence at Tarang Shakti as “another example of trust” between the two countries. France, a resident Indian Ocean power, fielded four Rafales, three A330 Phoenix aerial refuellers, two A400M transport aircraft and 300 personnel. This was part of its larger Pegase26 mission that set out on September 8, traveling across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific, Middle East and North Africa. Over 40 days across nine destinations and covering over 40,000 miles, the mission demonstrates its capacity for long-range deployment, sustenance and adaptability.

Exercises typically involve subject matter exchanges, and India, as the host nation, utilized this to brief visitors on the outcomes of Operation Sindoor of May 2025, which has generated significant operational lessons for military planners. Encapsulating this, Exercise Director Air Vice Marshal Raj Thakur noted that Operation Sindoor was one of the remarkable operations carried out by India, and there was a lot of interest in knowing about it. “And that’s why in one of the subject matter expert exchanges, we briefed them about what exactly has happened in Operation Sindoor and our part of the story, and that was very well received,” Thakur said.

India has had a very busy diplo-military calendar in recent years. These were quite often simultaneous engagements with nations that are warring or adversaries. To appreciate the busy calendar and the diversity of engagements by the Indian military, it is worth looking at some of the notable engagements since July.

The India-U.S. bilateral Army exercise Yudh Abhyas was conducted from September 15 to 27. It saw 600 personnel from each side exercise at a high-altitude area at Auli in Uttarakhand, followed by long-range firepower drills, including U.S. HIMARS, Indian Pinaka rocket systems, and counter-drone systems in action, at Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. Yudh Abhyas began in 2004 as a platoon-level exercise focused on peacekeeping operations and has since significantly expanded in scope and complexity. This is the case with all other India-U.S. military exercises: Cope India, the bilateral air exercise, or Exercise Malabar, which began as a bilateral naval exercise, have now become quadrilateral exercises featuring submarines and aircraft carriers practicing highly complex scenarios.

In addition to Yudh Abhyas, the Indian Army held bilateral wargames with Thailand (Maitree-XV), Mongolia (Nomadic Elephant), Kazakhstan (KAZIND) and UAE (Mountain Guardian), whether incoming or outgoing, with the last one set to conclude on October 18.

The Indian Navy has been the busiest with at least eight engagements. In addition to Indra, a trilateral exercise between India, Brazil and South Africa (Exercise IBSAMAR) is currently underway off South Africa. The Quad grouping, which includes India, Australia, Japan and the U.S., conducted a Tabletop Exercise on September 3 and 4 hosted by Japan to advance the Quad Indo-Pacific Logistics Network. In end-September, Quad Coast Guards carried out the second joint sail under the QUAD‑at‑Sea Ship Observer Mission. Indian Coast Guard Ship Shaunak sailed from Chennai on September 25 for Perth in Australia with six sea riders—t

analysis.tldr: India's massive multi-country military exercises show growing global defense trust, which supports long-term national security and steady economic ties without major domestic price shocks.
the_story: India hosted the second edition of the multilateral air exercise Tarang Shakti in Jodhpur from September 26 to October 12, themed 'Power in Partnership' with seven participating nations and 32 observing countries.
For the first time, U.S. fifth-generation F-35 fighter jets flew in Indian skies alongside Russian-origin Su-30MKIs, French Rafales, Indian LCAs, and UAE F-16s, completing over 800 sorties.

Simultaneously, India engaged in multiple other military drills, including the India-U.S. Yudh Abhyas army exercise in Uttarakhand and Rajasthan, and the India-Russia Indra naval exercise in Vladivostok from October 13 to 18.
analysis.what_happened: India successfully hosted large-scale international military exercises like Tarang Shakti and conducted simultaneous bilateral drills with global powers like the U.S. and Russia. These engagements highlight India's balanced foreign policy strategy of cooperating with multiple countries while maintaining its own strategic independence.
analysis.analogy: It is like a popular neighborhood store owner who maintains good, working relationships with competing suppliers across town, ensuring they can source the best tools from anyone without picking permanent sides.
why_it_matters_india: India conducts extensive joint military exercises with global partners like the U.S., Russia, France, and others.
This deepens military cooperation and builds technical trust across different nations' defense platforms.
Stronger strategic ties bolster overall national stability and trade confidence.
Stable regional security creates a predictable environment for domestic markets and foreign investments.

impacts.rationale: Broad geopolitical stability and strong defense partnerships provide a calm background for general market confidence — good for investors.
Increased focus on advanced military technology and joint exercises highlights the domestic defense sector's growth potential — generally positive for sector investors.

watch_next: Upcoming bilateral defense agreements and technology-sharing announcements
Future editions and participant lists of multilateral military exercises
analysis.caveats: Geopolitical military exercises are diplomatic and defense-focused events, meaning they rarely cause immediate shifts in daily consumer prices or financial markets.

events.headline: Awkward: Saudi Arabia’s new EV brand takes on the U.S. rival it already controls

items.title: Awkward: Saudi Arabia’s new EV brand takes on the U.S. rival it already controls
items.summary: The Exobot SUV by Ceer Motors

events.article_text:
Saudi Arabia’s first homegrown electric-vehicle maker is set to take on a U.S. rival the kingdom already controls.

Ceer Motors, majority-owned by the sovereign Public Investment Fund, revealed two electric car models on September 21, with deliveries promised for March 2027. The EVs were designed and engineered in Saudi Arabia, and will be built at Ceer’s plant in King Abdullah Economic City, north of Jeddah.

This is the PIF’s third EV bet. It bought about 5% of Tesla in 2018 and sold almost all of it by the end of 2019. It has also put about $8 billion into California-based Lucid, which has never turned a profit.

For the U.S., Ceer’s debut sets up an awkward rivalry: Saudi Arabia is building its own EV brand while its sovereign wealth fund owns a majority stake in Lucid, whose main factory is in Arizona. Ceer is PIF’s hedge against Lucid, whose shares have slumped more than 60% this year and whose Saudi sales are shrinking in a market dominated by China’s BYDiBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE.

“Lucid is an existing global technology and luxury-EV company in which Saudi Arabia has invested heavily,” Bill Russo, founder and CEO of Shanghai-based consulting firm Automobility, told Rest of World. “Ceer has a different mandate, creating a Saudi automotive OEM [original equipment manufacturer] and, importantly, an indigenous industrial ecosystem.”

Ceer, a venture between PIF and Taiwanese electronics maker Foxconn, was launched in November 2022. It had set 2025 as the target for its first cars.

Last week, the company’s CEO, James DeLuca, said Ceer will begin production early next year. Ceer has planned more models over the next five years, the company said at the launch. It also aims to make almost half the components of its cars locally by 2034.

Ceer’s Exobot sedan and an SUV are high-powered premium EVs — the segment where Lucid sells its Air luxury sedan and Gravity SUV. The most powerful Exobot versions promise more than 1,100 horsepower, DeLuca said, close to the 1,234 horsepower of Lucid’s fastest car, the Air Sapphire sedan. Ceer has yet to announce prices.

“That does put the initial products closer to Lucid’s premium territory than to BYD’s mass-market center of gravity,” Russo said.

The real test of its strategy will come when that range broadens, Russo said. Lucid, in which PIF holds about 58%, is already badly weakened. This year, it named a new CEO, Silvio Napoli; cut about a fifth of its U.S. workforce; ended its second production shift in Arizona; and recalled 27,000 sedans over a fire risk. Its market value has shrunk to about $1.6 billion.

In Saudi Arabia, Lucid’s sales fell 57% in the first seven months of 2026, while BYD’s rose 369%, according to estimates from Focus2Move, a Rome-based firm that tracks car sales in more than 150 countries. The gap partly reflects price, Hashim AlFatayerji, CEO of the independent Saudi advisory firm Cararak, told Rest of World.

“BYD and Lucid serve very different segments, so comparing their volumes directly can be misleading,” AlFatayerji said.

PIF has kept faith with Lucid through the slump. The carmaker remains one of only five U.S. companies in the fund’s latest quarterly holdings filing, and the Saudi government has agreed to buy up to 100,000 Lucid vehicles over 10 years.

Saudi Arabia has no official count of EV sales. Saudis buy almost 1 million new vehicles a year, and 10,000 to 20,000 of them are electric, AlFatayerji estimated. Joseph Salem, a senior partner who heads travel, transport, and hospitality at consulting firm Arthur D. Little in the Middle East and North Africa, puts the figure at 35,000 to 40,000 EVs in 2025, not counting plug-in hybrids.

Ceer’s factory is designed for as many as 240,000 vehicles a year, and Lucid already runs a smaller plant in the kingdom. That is far more than Saudi buyers can take, Salem told Rest of World.

“Combined, their full-capacity targets are roughly 10 times what the domestic market can plausibly absorb near-term,” he said. “So the majority of output, I’d say 80% plus, has to be export-oriented almost by design.”

Saudi Arabia is building a car industry sized for the Gulf, North Africa, and beyond, backed by PIF money and trade access across the region, Salem said. Exporting is the strategy, he said.

“The domestic market is the proving ground, not the end goal,” Salem said.

60% of the electric cars sold in the Middle East are from China’s BYD.

Abroad, Ceer will meet Chinese rivals that already lead the region. In the Middle East, BYD sells about 60% of electric cars and Tesla about 15%, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook.

Chinese carmakers pose a tougher test, Russo said. They have spent years building huge factories, close ties with suppliers, and the ability to sell cheaply, and are now expanding abroad because they can make more cars than China can absorb, he said.

Ceer relies on established suppliers for key parts. Its motors come from Croatia’s Rimac and South Korea’s Hyundai Transys, while its platform is from Taiwan’s Foxconn. It has licensed some component technology from BMW.

“A new entrant cannot simply license its way to that level of competitiveness,” Russo said.

To win buyers at home and abroad, Ceer must match BYD on price, using local parts and state-backed financing, Salem said. It also needs a dealer and service network as wide as BYD’s from the outset, and cars that stand out on their own merits beyond being made in Saudi Arabia, he said.

“It’s a high bar,” Salem said. “But Ceer has the capital and policy backing to close that gap faster than a typical new entrant would.”

Ceer has advantages few new carmakers get, including long-term funding, a powerful backer at home, and the freedom to build on proven technology from others, said Russo. What it still has to earn is a brand that wins customers on

analysis.tldr: Saudi Arabia's push to build its own electric vehicle industry could reshape global car supply chains, indirectly influencing how Indian auto component makers secure international tech partnerships.
the_story: Saudi Arabia's first homegrown electric-vehicle brand, Ceer Motors, revealed two electric car models on September 21, with deliveries promised for March 2027.
Ceer is a joint venture between Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF), and Taiwanese electronics maker Foxconn, launched in November 2022.
The PIF also owns a majority stake (about 58%) in the troubled U.S. electric-vehicle maker Lucid, making Ceer a state-backed rival to a company the kingdom already controls.
Ceer's factory in King Abdullah Economic City is designed to make up to 240,000 vehicles a year, meaning over 80% of its production will need to be exported because local demand is much lower.
analysis.what_happened: Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund is launching a new local electric vehicle brand called Ceer Motors to build a domestic car industry. This move comes as its previous major U.S. electric vehicle investment, Lucid, struggles with shrinking sales in Saudi Arabia, steep share price drops, and global competition from China's BYD. Because the local Saudi market is too small to buy all the cars Ceer plans to make, the company is designed to export most of its vehicles abroad.
analysis.analogy: It is like a wealthy landlord who built a luxury hotel franchise, but seeing it struggle, decides to build a brand-new, competing hotel chain down the street using his own deep pockets, aiming to sell rooms to people all over the world.
why_it_matters_india: Saudi Arabia's sovereign fund invests heavily in global manufacturing, technology, and electric vehicle ecosystems.
New state-backed global players look for international partnerships for parts, technology, and engineering.
Indian auto-component manufacturers compete or collaborate within global supply chains for electric vehicles.
Shifts in global electric vehicle pricing and manufacturing capacity ripple outward to emerging market supply networks.

impacts.target: Auto component stocks in India (like Motherson Sumi, Bosch, etc.)
impacts.rationale: More global electric vehicle brands entering the market could increase overall demand for international parts suppliers, though Ceer currently relies on partners from Taiwan, Croatia, and South Korea.
Saudi Arabia's aggressive push into electric vehicles underscores the long-term global transition away from oil, which could eventually lower oil prices—a relief for India as a major oil importer.

watch_next: Whether Ceer meets its March 2027 delivery target for its electric vehicles.
How the Saudi fund manages its financial support between its struggling U.S. investment Lucid and its new domestic brand Ceer.
analysis.caveats: The article focuses entirely on Saudi Arabia's domestic strategy and its ties to U.S. and Chinese competitors, meaning direct links to Indian markets depend entirely on broader global supply chain shifts.

history.title: A bank run at the speed of a smartphone
history.what: Silicon Valley Bank lost $42 billion of deposits in a single day and was shut by regulators within about 48 hours of the first sign of trouble — the fastest bank run in history.
history.why: The bank had taken enormous deposits during the technology boom and put them into long-dated government bonds, which carry no credit risk at all. When rates rose sharply in 2022, those bonds lost market value. The holdings were fine if held to maturity and not if it had to sell — and over 90% of its deposits were above the insured limit, so depositors had every reason to run first and ask later. Word spread through group chats.
history.impact: Two more US banks failed within days, and Credit Suisse — unrelated but fragile — was forced into a shotgun merger. Bank shares fell worldwide. Gold rose, as it does whenever people start questioning banks.
history.policy: US regulators guaranteed all deposits at the failed banks, insured or not, and opened a facility letting banks borrow against bonds at face value rather than market value. Supervision of mid-sized banks was tightened.
history.consequence: The rule that only insured deposits are protected was effectively suspended in practice, which stores up its own future problem. It also made interest-rate risk, rather than credit risk, the first thing bank supervisors now ask about.
history.pattern: A government bond has no default risk and plenty of price risk, and that distinction stays invisible until somebody is forced to sell. Meanwhile concentrated, uninsured depositors are the modern queue outside the door — and they move in minutes now, not days.
history.india_echo: Indian deposits are insured only to ₹5 lakh per bank, which is exactly why that limit is flagged under cash on the Asset Classes page. Indian banks hold large government bond portfolios too, though with far stickier retail deposits behind them.
history.watch_for: Banks with depositors concentrated in one industry, and large unrealised losses on bonds held to maturity. Both are disclosed if you look for them.
